Millar Western Forest Products Ltd. will indefinitely curtail operations at its Quesnel River Pulp mill, citing market conditions and uncertainty surrounding economic fibre supply. The *Quesnel Cariboo Observer* obtained a copy of a letter sent out on Nov. 9, to employees at the Quesnel River Pulp mill. In the letter, executive chair and CEO Karl Meyers said the company had made the “very difficult decision” to curtail Quesnel River Pulp mill for an indefinite period. “Based on current contractual obligations, we will continue operating the effluent system for twelve months, or until we can reach an acceptable alternative,” Meyers said in the letter. “We will continue to complete an orderly shutdown of the balance of the operations over the next several weeks, setting it up for a potential restart in the future.” In August, Millar Western announced temporary curtailment of operations until at least November. According to the letter, the duration of the curtailment remains unknown and will depend on market conditions and the availability of economic fibre supply. “As a result, we will be terminating employment for all those impacted and providing severance compensation and other support,” Meyers wrote. He added the company will also provide continuation of certain benefits and access to employee and family assistance resources, with details to be outlined in individual severance letters. Meyers said Millar Western will also look at filling vacancies at other company operations with displaced employees. “For those who will continue to work, the period between now and your final day of employment will be considered as working notice,” he said. According to the letter, to qualify for severance, employees must remain active until their last scheduled day of work.

France’s protest movement over living costs, wages and public services has spread to 30 other European countries, with more than 1,700 demonstrations recorded across the continent from Sept. 15 to Oct. 30, according to an analysis of Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (ACLED) figures. In France, the protests began with students challenging school conditions and widened to include unions and other groups. On Saturday, Nov. 7, the Interior Ministry counted 146,000 demonstrators nationwide, including 46,000 in Paris; unions estimated 250,000 and 75,000, respectively. It was the fourth consecutive Saturday of protests, and clashes followed in Paris and other cities. French authorities deployed about 70,000 security personnel on Saturday. The Interior Ministry recorded at least 360 arrests nationwide, according to AFP. Attendance was down from earlier weekends and from Thursday’s union rally, which drew 575,000 people by the government’s count. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu is due to meet labor unions and employer representatives on Monday, Nov. 9, to discuss wages and purchasing power. Student and teacher groups have called for a strike on Tuesday, while France’s Senate is scheduled to begin debating the government’s 2027 budget proposal on Nov. 20.

items.title: [dagenslantbruk.se] Farmers urged to tailor grazing to grassland recovery and climate
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Agricultural specialists in Sweden, France and South Africa say grassland management requires continued upkeep and grazing adapted to local vegetation and weather. Sweden’s inventory found that the natural and cultural values of most re-surveyed meadows and pastures remained broadly stable, while French livestock farmers discussed how the 2026 drought and heat affected forage production. University of Limpopo pasture scientist Lesego Motshekga says rotational grazing works only when stocking rates match available forage and plants have time to recover; moving animals between camps alone cannot prevent overgrazing. Motshekga recommends deciding when to move livestock based on grass condition rather than a fixed calendar.

items.title: [scitechdaily.com] Researchers identify new dinosaur genus from fossil found in England in 2001
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Paleontologists have classified a fossil found in a Surrey clay quarry in 2001 as Paludohadros proudlovii, a previously unknown genus and species of plant-eating dinosaur that lived about 125 million years ago. The four-legged animal was about 5 metres long and weighed an estimated 1.5 to 2 metric tons, but its bones indicate it had not reached adulthood. The fossil was donated to London’s Natural History Museum, where it remained for years before a detailed comparison with other iguanodontians revealed distinguishing features. The identification also helped researchers identify fossils collected from the same quarry in the 1950s as belonging to the newly named dinosaur. NASA said Swift detected about 20,000 ultraviolet sources there, many of them hot stars and star clusters obscured in visible-light views. Swift was designed to turn rapidly toward short-lived cosmic explosions and observe them in optical, ultraviolet and X-ray light. It also alerted other observatories so they could follow events before they faded. The U.S. Space Force said Swift reentered the atmosphere at 7:39 a.m. EST over North Sumatra. NASA expected most of the spacecraft to burn up, though some pieces may have survived.

items.title: [abc.net.au] Lancet researchers urge health emergency declaration as climate losses mount
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Heat-related disruption cost the world an estimated $1.07 trillion in lost worker productivity in 2025, while extreme drought affected about 52% of global land for at least a month, according to the 2026 Lancet Countdown report. The report’s 146 researchers from 30 countries urged governments to treat climate change as a global health emergency and coordinate a sustained response. Extreme rainfall affected 17.2% of global land each year from 2016 to 2025, up from 14.8% in the preceding decade, and the researchers linked shifting groundwater conditions to risks for food security and sanitation. Southeast Asia and Africa suffered the largest productivity-related economic losses, equivalent to 3.9% and 3.2% of gross domestic product, respectively. Clean-energy investment reached $2.1 trillion in 2025, nearly twice fossil-fuel investment, but fossil fuels still supplied more than 80% of global energy. The report calls for governments to consider health in climate decisions and direct climate and health funding to vulnerable countries. Researchers are expected to press the issue at the COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Türkiye, scheduled for Nov. 9-20.

items.title: [phys.org] Researchers document sustained sexual bond between Ethiopian bull and male donkey
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

An Italian-led research team documented repeated sexual interactions between a bull and a male donkey on an Ethiopian plateau, describing a selective social bond between the animals. During eight days of observation in March 2026, the bull, Achilles, mounted the donkey, Patroclus, 51 times; 34 mountings involved penetration. The findings appeared Nov. 2 in the journal Current Biology. The pair also licked, rubbed and nuzzled one another, and researchers repeatedly saw them seek each other out despite access to other potential mates. The team cautions that observations of one domesticated pair cannot establish why the behavior occurred or what the animals felt. Dry-season conditions led herders to move them to separate pastures; researchers in Ethiopia are trying to arrange a reunion to observe whether their interactions resume.

items.title: [cbsnews.com] US strikes Iran’s Qeshm Island as Tehran talks continue
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

The United States struck targets on Iran’s Qeshm Island on Monday, Nov. 2, U.S. officials said, describing the limited operation as defensive and aimed at Iranian forces using surface-to-air missiles against U.S. assets. One U.S. official said the action followed Iranian fire at an American aircraft; Iranian state media reported five explosions on the island and said residents saw two aircraft overhead. The Wall Street Journal reported that the strike was part of a series of smaller, previously undisclosed U.S. attacks in recent weeks. Officials said the operations were intended to counter threats to U.S. forces and commercial shipping without signaling that Washington was resuming major combat. The Strait of Hormuz, where shipping has been heavily disrupted since the war began in February, is a key oil route. Oil prices fell more than 7% on Monday as expectations of a deal grew. President Donald Trump said a settlement with Tehran “could happen,” and Vice President JD Vance said talks had made progress. Iran’s foreign minister said indirect discussions were underway through mediators. U.S. officials said further talks were planned this week to pursue a framework linking an end to Iranian attacks in the strait with the lifting of the U.S. blockade on Iranian ports.
